 Quit
India Movement
 
After the failure of the Cripps Mission, Mahatma Gandhi decided to launch
his third major movement against British rule. This was the “Quit India”
campaign, which began in August 1942. Although Gandhiji was jailed at
once, younger activists organised strikes and acts of sabotage all over the
country. Particularly active in the underground resistance were socialist
members of the Congress, such as Jayaprakash Narayan. In several
districts, such as Satara in the west and Medinipur in the east,
“independent” governments were proclaimed. The British responded with
much force, yet it took more than a year to suppress the rebellion. “Quit
India” was genuinely a mass movement, bringing into its ambit hundreds
of thousands of ordinary Indians. It especially energised the young who, in
very large numbers, left their colleges to go to jail. However, while the
Congress leaders languished in jail, Jinnah and his colleagues in the
Muslim League worked patiently at expanding their influence. It was in
these years that the League began to make a mark in the Punjab and Sind,
provinces where it had previously had scarcely any presence. In 1943,
some of the younger leaders in the Satara district of Maharashtra set up a

topic: Gandhi's Peace Mission in Riot-Torn Bengal
questionText:
Read the following excerpt carefully and answer the question that follows:

"On 15 August 1947, as festivities erupted in New Delhi to celebrate Indian independence, Mahatma Gandhi was in Calcutta, staying in an abandoned Muslim mansion (Hydari Mansion in Beliaghata). He did not attend the midnight celebrations in Parliament, nor did he hoist the national flag. Instead, he observed a 24-hour fast and prayed for communal harmony. Riots had convulsed Bengal since the Great Calcutta Killings of August 1946. Gandhi walked barefoot from village to village in Noakhali and fasted in Calcutta, dousing the fires of communal hatred. Admiring his moral courage, Viceroy Lord Mountbatten wrote to him: 'In the Punjab we have 55,000 soldiers and large-scale riots on our hands; in Bengal our force consists of one man, and there is no rioting. As a serving officer, may I be allowed to pay my tribute to the One-Man Boundary Army.'"

What military title did Viceroy Lord Mountbatten bestow upon Mahatma Gandhi in his letter of tribute?

options.text: 'The One-Man Boundary Army'
options.mistakeAnalysis: Correct answer. Accurately identifies the verified NCERT concept for Gandhi's Peace Mission in Riot-Torn Bengal.

detailedSolution:
Detailed Solution:
According to NCERT principles for Mahatma Gandhi and National Movement (Gandhi's Peace Mission in Riot-Torn Bengal):
'The One-Man Boundary Army'
